questions.q: What's wrong with framing NoSQL as 'relational data with the constraints removed', per this lesson?
options: It misses that document/graph models are built around a real architectural bet — matching how data is actually read or related, not just skipping schema design
Nothing is wrong with that framing — it's accurate
NoSQL databases actually enforce more constraints than relational databases
This framing only applies to Neo4j, not MongoDB
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns this framing is wrong and will actively mislead — NoSQL solves a different problem, not a lazier version of the same problem.

questions.q: Why does this course cover Azure Cosmos DB specifically, per this lesson?
options: It's the natural next step after this catalog's SQL Server/Azure DBA content, and a real Azure DBA increasingly needs it — one engine with multiple APIs, designed for multi-region distribution
Cosmos DB is a relational database like SQL Server
Cosmos DB has no connection to anything else in this catalog
Cosmos DB is being deprecated, so this is a farewell lesson
questions.explain: Cosmos DB is framed as a genuine extension of the Azure DBA skill set already built earlier in this catalog.

questions.q: What is the key difference in how a graph database like Neo4j stores relationships, compared to a relational database?
options: Relationships are first-class, stored objects — not reconstructed at query time via a JOIN
Graph databases have no concept of relationships at all
Relationships in Neo4j work identically to foreign keys in SQL Server
Graph databases store relationships exactly the same way relational databases do
questions.explain: Relationships are stored directly, not derived through a JOIN operation at query time — a genuine architectural difference.

questions.q: What mental shift does NoSQL data modeling generally require, compared to relational design, per this lesson?
options: Starting from the actual access pattern (what's read together, how often) and shaping data to match it, rather than normalizing first and joining at read time
There is no real difference in approach between the two
NoSQL modeling always requires MORE normalization than relational design
NoSQL modeling ignores how data will be read entirely
questions.explain: This reverses the typical relational order: understand the read pattern first, then shape (often denormalize) the data to match it.

questions.q: What honest tradeoffs does this lesson say NoSQL modeling comes with?
options: Data duplication, eventual consistency, and harder ad hoc querying
There are no real tradeoffs — NoSQL is strictly better in every case
NoSQL databases are always slower than relational databases
NoSQL requires more storage but has no other real tradeoffs
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly commits to covering these tradeoffs honestly rather than glossing over them.
